claim: MS-Hu6 is a first-in-class FSH-blocking humanized antibody proposed for clinical use in osteoporosis, obesity, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Here, we report the development of a unique formulation for our first-in-class FSH-blocking humanized antibody, MS-Hu6, which we propose to move to the clinic for osteoporosis, obesity, and Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: The abstract states the antibody type and proposed clinical indications.

claim: The studies were carried out using a Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) platform compliant with Code of Federal Regulations (Title 21, Part 58).
source: The studies were carried out using our Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) platform, compliant with the Code of Federal Regulations (Title 21, Part 58).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the regulatory compliance framework used.

claim: Thermal, monomeric, and colloidal stability of formulated MS-Hu6 was maintained at a concentration of 100 mg/mL.
source: We found that thermal, monomeric, and colloidal stability of formulated MS-Hu6 was maintained at a concentration of 100 mg/mL.
evidence: The abstract reports findings from protein thermal shift, size exclusion chromatography, and dynamic light scattering experiments.

claim: Addition of L-methionine and disodium EDTA improved the formulation's long-term colloidal and thermal stability.
source: The addition of the antioxidant L-methionine and chelating agent disodium EDTA improved the formulation's long-term colloidal and thermal stability.
evidence: The abstract states the effect of these excipients on stability.

claim: Physiochemical properties of formulated MS-Hu6, including viscosity, turbidity, and clarity, conformed with acceptable industry standards.
source: Physiochemical properties of formulated MS-Hu6, including viscosity, turbidity, and clarity, confirmed with acceptable industry standards.
evidence: The abstract reports conformance with industry standards for these properties.

claim: The structural integrity of MS-Hu6 in formulation was maintained as proven through Circular Dichroism (CD) and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy.
source: That the structural integrity of MS-Hu6 in formulation was maintained was proven through Circular Dichroism (CD) and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy.
evidence: The abstract reports structural analysis results from CD and FTIR.

claim: Three rapid freeze–thaw cycles at –80 °C/25 °C or –80 °C/37 °C revealed excellent thermal and colloidal stability.
source: Three rapid freeze–thaw cycles at –80 °C/25 °C or –80 °C/37 °C further revealed excellent thermal and colloidal stability.
evidence: The abstract reports results from freeze-thaw stability testing.

claim: Formulated MS-Hu6, particularly its Fab domain, displayed thermal and monomeric storage stability for more than 90 days at 4°C and 25°C.
source: Furthermore, formulated MS-Hu6, particularly its Fab domain, displayed thermal and monomeric storage stability for more than 90 days at 4°C and 25°C.
evidence: The abstract reports accelerated stability study results.

claim: The unfolding temperature (Tm) for formulated MS-Hu6 increased by >4.80 °C upon binding to recombinant FSH.
source: Finally, the unfolding temperature (Tm) for formulated MS-Hu6 increased by >4.80 °C upon binding to recombinant FSH, indicating highly specific ligand binding.
evidence: The abstract reports the Tm shift upon FSH binding.

claim: The Tm shift upon FSH binding indicates highly specific ligand binding.
source: Finally, the unfolding temperature (Tm) for formulated MS-Hu6 increased by >4.80 °C upon binding to recombinant FSH, indicating highly specific ligand binding.
evidence: The abstract interprets the Tm shift as evidence of specific binding.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies have witnessed the most rapid growth in biotherapeutics because of their specificity and adaptability.
source: Biotherapeutics have transformed the treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases and cancers (Lu et al., 2020; Passot et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021), with monoclonal antibodies witnessing the most rapid growth because of their specificity and adaptability (An, 2010; Shire et al., 2004; Whitaker et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references supporting this statement.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies, particularly blocking antibodies, are generally of low affinity and must be administered at relatively high doses to elicit therapeutic responses.
source: As monoclonal antibodies, particularly blocking antibodies, are generally of low affinity, and therefore must be administered at relatively high doses to elicit therapeutic responses (Whitaker et al., 2017; Elbakri et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this statement about blocking antibodies.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies are mostly given subcutaneously at a maximally allowable volume of 1.5 mL.
source: Mostly given subcutaneously (Wang et al., 2021), they are utilized at a maximally allowable volume of 1.5 mL.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this administration parameter.

claim: It has become critical to develop formulations of monoclonal antibodies at ultra-high concentrations.
source: It has therefore become critical to develop formulations of monoclonal antibodies at ultra-high concentrations (Wang et al., 2021; Storz, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this need.

claim: Ultra-high concentration formulations allow single-dose self-administration using auto-injection devices, reduced dosing frequency, and improved patient compliance.
source: These formulations also allow single-dose self-administration using auto-injection devices, reduced dosing frequency, and improved patient compliance (Wang et al., 2021; BioProcess International, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting these benefits.

claim: Ultra-high concentration monoclonal antibody formulations are associated with physical and chemical instabilities depending on the physicochemical properties of the specific monoclonal antibody.
source: However, ultra-high concentration monoclonal antibody formulations are associated with physical and chemical instabilities depending on the physicochemical properties of the specific monoclonal antibody (Bramham et al., 2021; Jiskoot et al., 2022; Klich et al., 2023).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this challenge.

claim: Highly concentrated formulations may be very viscous or gelatinous, leading to increased tissue back pressure and pain at the injection site.
source: Notably, due to the higher concentrations, these formulations may be very viscous or gelatinous, leading to increased tissue back pressure and pain at the injection site (Whitaker et al., 2017; Jezek et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this problem.

claim: Manufacturing challenges for highly concentrated formulations include difficulty in pumping due to high shear stress, clogging of the membrane, high back pressure, and aggregation during manufacturing.
source: Manufacturing challenges for highly concentrated formulations also include difficulty in pumping due to high shear stress, clogging of the membrane, high back pressure, and aggregation during the manufacturing (Thomas et al., 1979; Bee et al., 2009; Hung et al., 2016; Goswami et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting these manufacturing challenges.

claim: 34 out of 103 monoclonal antibody therapeutics approved by the U.S. FDA have been developed with high protein concentrations (≥100 mg/mL).
source: Despite these obstacles, 34 out of 103 monoclonal antibody therapeutics approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), that constitute almost one third of all approved biotherapeutics, have been developed with high protein concentrations (≥100 mg/mL); 76% of the approved formulations are administered by the subcutaneous route (Wang et al., 2021; Storz, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references for these FDA approval statistics.

claim: 76% of approved high-concentration monoclonal antibody formulations are administered by the subcutaneous route.
source: Despite these obstacles, 34 out of 103 monoclonal antibody therapeutics approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), that constitute almost one third of all approved biotherapeutics, have been developed with high protein concentrations (≥100 mg/mL); 76% of the approved formulations are administered by the subcutaneous route (Wang et al., 2021; Storz, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this administration route statistic.

claim: Palivizumab (Synagis, 100 mg/mL) was the first ultra-high concentration monoclonal antibody formulation approved in 1998.
source: The very first ultra–high concentration monoclonal antibody formulation, Palivizumab (Synagis, 100 mg/mL), was approved in 1998 (Geskey et al., 2007), followed by others including Alirocumab (150 mg/mL, Sanofi–Regeneron), Cosentyx (150 mg/mL, Novartis), Actemra (180 mg/mL, Genentech), and Belimumab (200 mg/mL, GlaxoSmithKline) (Lu et al., 2020; Whitaker et al., 2017; Baldo, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this historical approval.

claim: The main issue with highly concentrated formulations is protein–protein interactions resulting from high viscosity and a crowded environment.
source: The main issue with highly concentrated formulations is protein–protein interactions (Shire et al., 2004; BioProcess International, 2014) resulting from high viscosity and a crowded environment (Whitaker et al., 2017; Buck et al., 2015; Arora et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites references supporting this main issue.

claim: Protein-protein interactions may cause undesirable liquid–liquid separation, protein aggregation, or opalescence.
source: Such interactions are reversible or irreversible, and may cause undesirable liquid–liquid separation, protein aggregation, or opalescence (Whitaker et al., 2017; Ratanji et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites references for these consequences.

claim: Protein-protein interactions may be caused by hydrophobic, electrostatic, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding, or van der Waals interactions.
source: The effects may also be caused by a variety of transient interactions in the solution, including hydrophobic, electrostatic, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding (inter and intra), or van der Waals interactions (Esfandiary et al., 2015; Connolly et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2014) via Fab-Fab (Buck et al., 2015) or, in rare instances, Fab-Fc (Arora et al., 2016) interactions between antibodies.
evidence: The introduction cites references for these interaction types.

claim: Proteins generally undergo aggregation using native monomers, denatured proteins, and pre-existing aggregates.
source: Proteins generally undergo aggregation using native monomers, denatured proteins, and pre-existing aggregates (Goswami et al., 2013; Narhi et al., 2012; Pham and Meng, 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites references for aggregation mechanisms.

claim: Native monomers self-associate into oligomers through transient interactions and regain their native structure, resulting in reversible aggregates.
source: Native monomers self-associate into the oligomers through transient interactions and regain their native structure—most such associations result in reversible aggregates.
evidence: The introduction describes this aggregation pathway.

claim: Upon stressing and over time, monomers can associate to form multimers, resulting in irreversible (insoluble) aggregates.
source: However, upon stressing, and over time, monomers can associate to form multimers, resulting in irreversible (insoluble) aggregates (Ratanji et al., 2016; Pham and Meng, 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this aggregation pathway.

claim: 5–10% soluble aggregates are acceptable for biologic therapeutics.
source: While 5–10% soluble aggregates are acceptable for biologic therapeutics, insoluble aggregates must be limited for stable formulations (Pham and Meng, 2020; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this acceptability threshold.

claim: Insoluble aggregates must be limited for stable formulations.
source: While 5–10% soluble aggregates are acceptable for biologic therapeutics, insoluble aggregates must be limited for stable formulations (Pham and Meng, 2020; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this requirement.

claim: The US Pharmacopeia (USP) and the FDA have set guidelines to control aggregates in a final biologic formulation.
source: The US Pharmacopeia (USP) and the FDA have set guidelines to control aggregates in a final biologic formulation (U.S Food and Drug Administration, 2021; USP, 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites regulatory guidelines.

claim: Sub-visible particles with a hydrodynamic radius ≤50–100 µm are considered optimal.
source: For example, sub–visible particles with a hydrodynamic radius ≤50–100 µm are considered optimal (Ratanji et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this particle size guideline.

claim: Per the FDA, the acceptable limit of subvisible particulate matter in a container of ≤100 mL should be 6000 particles ≥10 μm and 600 particles ≥25 μm.
source: Hence, per the FDA, the acceptable limit of subvisible particulate matter in a container of ≤100 mL should be 6000 particles ≥10 μm and 600 particles ≥25 μm (Ratanji et al., 2016; Pham and Meng, 2020; U.S Food and Drug Administration, 2021; Pham and Meng, 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites FDA guidelines for particulate matter limits.

claim: Particle sizes ≤10 μm can cause vascular occlusion.
source: Particle sizes ≤10 μm can cause vascular occlusion.
evidence: The introduction states this clinical consequence.

claim: MS-Hu6 is a humanized FSH-blocking antibody developed based on studies establishing direct actions of FSH in promoting bone loss, body fat accrual, and neurodegeneration.
source: We have reported the development of a first-of-its-kind humanized FSH-blocking antibody, MS-Hu6, based on studies that have established direct actions of FSH in promoting bone loss, body fat accrual, and neurodegeneration.
evidence: The introduction describes the rationale for MS-Hu6 development.

claim: MS-Hu6 reduces body fat, induces thermogenic adipose tissue, improves bone density, and prevents cognitive decline in mouse models.
source: MS-Hu6 reduces body fat, induces thermogenic adipose tissue, improves bone density, and prevents cognitive decline in mouse models (Gera et al., 2020; Zaidi et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2012; Gera et al., 2022; Zaidi et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for these preclinical effects.

claim: MS-Hu6 was humanized from the parent murine antibody clone, Hf2, generated against a short 13-amino-acid-long epitope of the receptor-binding sequence of FSHβ.
source: MS-Hu6 was humanized from the parent murine antibody clone, Hf2, generated against a short 13-amino-acid-long epitope of the receptor-binding sequence of FSHβ (Ji et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for the antibody's origin.

claim: MS-Hu6 binds to FSHβ and blocks its interaction with the FSH receptor (FSHR) with an affinity of 7.5 nM.
source: We have shown that MS-Hu6 binds to FSHβ and blocks its interaction with the FSH receptor (FSHR) with an affinity of 7.5 nM, comparable to trastuzumab (KD ~5 nM, Herceptin; Gera et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this binding affinity.

claim: MS-Hu6's affinity for FSHβ (7.5 nM) is comparable to trastuzumab's affinity (KD ~5 nM).
source: We have shown that MS-Hu6 binds to FSHβ and blocks its interaction with the FSH receptor (FSHR) with an affinity of 7.5 nM, comparable to trastuzumab (KD ~5 nM, Herceptin; Gera et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this comparison.

claim: A low-concentration formulation for MS-Hu6 was previously reported.
source: We have recently reported a low-concentration formulation for MS-Hu6 (Sant et al., 2023).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for prior work.

claim: The previously reported low-concentration MS-Hu6 formulation consisted of 0.15 mg/mL of MS-Hu6, 20 mM phosphate buffer (pH 6.2), 1 mM sodium chloride, 0.001% w/v Tween 20 and 260 mM sucrose.
source: This optimized formulation consisted of 0.15 mg/mL of MS-Hu6, 20 mM phosphate buffer (pH 6.2), 1 mM sodium chloride, 0.001% w/v Tween 20 and 260 mM sucrose.
evidence: The introduction describes the composition of the prior formulation.

claim: Tm values for the Fc and Fab domains of MS-Hu6 in PBS at 1 mg/mL were 69.17 ± 0.02 °C and 79.64 ± 0.02 °C, respectively.
source: Tm values for the Fc and Fab domains of MS-Hu6 in PBS at 1 mg/mL were 69.17 ± 0.02 °C and 79.64 ± 0.02 °C, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports these measured Tm values.

claim: Tm values increased progressively up to 10 and 20 mg/mL for the Fab and Fc regions of formulated MS-Hu6 compared with MS-Hu6 in PBS.
source: Increases Tm values compared with MS-Hu6 in PBS were noted progressively up to 10 and 20 mg/mL for the Fab and Fc regions of formulated MS-Hu6.
evidence: The results section reports this trend in Tm values.

claim: At higher concentrations (50 and 100 mg/mL), while Tm values dropped somewhat for the MS-Hu6 formulation compared with MS-Hu6 in PBS, the difference (or ΔTm) did not exceed 1 °C.
source: However, at higher concentrations (50 and 100 mg/mL), while Tm values dropped somewhat for the MS-Hu6 formulation compared with MS-Hu6 in PBS, the difference (or ΔTm) did not exceed 1 °C—which provided assurance of thermostability even at 100 mg/mL.
evidence: The results section reports these Tm differences and interprets them.

claim: MS-Hu6 in PBS or in formulation exists mainly in its monomeric form (>99%) with a dimer area of <1%.
source: Figure 1B shows that MS-Hu6 in PBS or in formulation exists mainly in its monomeric form (>99%) with a dimer area of <1%; the latter is within acceptable industry standards of <3–5%.
evidence: The results section references Figure 1B showing SEC data.

claim: A dimer area of <1% is within acceptable industry standards of <3–5%.
source: Figure 1B shows that MS-Hu6 in PBS or in formulation exists mainly in its monomeric form (>99%) with a dimer area of <1%; the latter is within acceptable industry standards of <3–5%.
evidence: The results section compares the measured dimer area to industry standards.

claim: MS-Hu6 (in PBS) samples displayed a prominent peak (volume %~99%) with an average rh of 4.96 nm.
source: The two MS-Hu6 (in PBS) samples displayed a prominent peak (volume %~99%) with an average rh of 4.96 nm, which fell within the industry standard (rh <10 nm).
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 1C.

claim: An rh of 4.96 nm falls within the industry standard (rh <10 nm).
source: The two MS-Hu6 (in PBS) samples displayed a prominent peak (volume %~99%) with an average rh of 4.96 nm, which fell within the industry standard (rh <10 nm).
evidence: The results section compares the measured rh to industry standards.

claim: MS-Hu6 in PBS had two aggregated peaks with average volume percentages of <1%, but with an average rh of 91.4 and 2595 nm, respectively.
source: However, there were two aggregated peaks with average volume percentages of <1%, but with an average rh of 91.4 and 2595 nm, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 1C.

claim: MS-Hu6 formulations containing 1 and 50 mg/mL MS-Hu6 displayed 99–100 volume % in a single peak, with average rh values of ~4 nm.
source: In contrast, MS-Hu6 formulations containing 1 and 50 mg/mL MS-Hu6 displayed 99–100 volume % in a single peak, with average rh values of ~4 nm.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 1C.

claim: In the 100 mg/mL formulation, a negligible peak (0.1% in sample 3) was associated with a large rh of 2671 nm.
source: In the 100 mg/mL formulation, however, a negligible peak (0.1% in sample 3) was associated with a large rh of 2671 nm, whereas the other samples (1 and 2) displayed single peaks with an average rh of 3.68 nm.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 1C.

claim: PDI values in all MS-Hu6 formulation cases were <1, which is the accepted cut-off.
source: Nonetheless, the PDI values in all cases were <1, which is the accepted cut-off.
evidence: The results section compares PDI values to the accepted cut-off.

claim: Large particles with high rh values can form as soluble reversible aggregates, which are well accepted in biotherapeutics development at levels <10%.
source: Large particles with a high rh values can form as soluble reversible aggregates, which are well accepted in biotherapeutics development at levels <10%.
evidence: The results section states this acceptability threshold.

claim: Formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) plus 1 mM EDTA and 1 mM L-methionine showed a slight increased ΔTm value for the Fc domain of 0.38 °C compared with MS-Hu6 (8.621 mg/mL) in PBS.
source: Protein thermal shift showed that compared with MS-Hu6 (8.621 mg/mL) in PBS, formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) plus 1 mM EDTA and 1 mM L-methionine showed slight increased ΔTm value for the Fc domain of 0.38 °C (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section reports protein thermal shift data from Figure 2A.

claim: The addition of EDTA and L-methionine suggests that methionine oxidation and catalytic oxidation were being prevented to enhance the thermostability of MS-Hu6.
source: This suggested that methionine oxidation and catalytic oxidation were being prevented to enhance the thermostability of MS-Hu6.
evidence: The results section interprets the Tm shift as evidence of oxidation prevention.

claim: There was no significant Tm shift in the Fab domain upon EDTA or L-methionine addition.
source: In contrast, there was no significant Tm shift in the Fab domain upon EDTA or L-methionine addition.
evidence: The results section reports this observation.

claim: MS-Hu6 at 8.621 mg/mL in PBS displayed a major peak (98.6% volume) with an average rh of 5.43 nm.
source: MS-Hu6 at 8.621 mg/mL in PBS displayed a major peak (98.6% volume) with an average rh of 5.43 nm, which fell within the industry standard (rh <10 nm).
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 2B.

claim: MS-Hu6 at 8.621 mg/mL in PBS had two minor aggregated peaks with <1.5% total volume, but with an average rh of 86.8 and 2400 nm, respectively.
source: However, there were two minor aggregated peaks with <1.5% total volume, but with an average rh of 86.8 and 2400 nm, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 2B.

claim: Formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) displayed a main peak at a rh value of 5.75 nm with a 99.3% volume.
source: In contrast, formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) displayed a main peak at a rh value of 5.75 nm with a higher, 99.3% volume; this size was consistent with the reported literature (Akbas et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 2B and cites a reference for comparison.

claim: Formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) had two minor peaks with <0.5% volume and rh values of 748 and 2631 nm, respectively.
source: There were two minor peaks with <0.5% volume and rh values of 748 and 2631 nm, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 2B.

claim: The addition of disodium-EDTA and L-methionine to the formulation, at 0.5 mM or 1 mM each, reduced the volume of the aggregated peaks and resulted in main peaks with near–100% volume.
source: The addition of disodium-EDTA and L-methionine to the formulation, at 0.5 mM or 1 mM each, both within the IIG limit (Zhou et al., 2012; Rayaprolu et al., 2018; Stadtman, 1990), reduced the volume of the aggregated peaks and resulted in main peaks with near–100% volume, respectively.
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 2B and cites references for IIG limits.

claim: 0.5 mM or 1 mM each of disodium-EDTA and L-methionine are within the IIG limit.
source: The addition of disodium-EDTA and L-methionine to the formulation, at 0.5 mM or 1 mM each, both within the IIG limit (Zhou et al., 2012; Rayaprolu et al., 2018; Stadtman, 1990), reduced the volume of the aggregated peaks and resulted in main peaks with near–100% volume, respectively.
evidence: The results section cites references for IIG limits.

claim: Disodium-EDTA and L-methionine together improved colloidal stability, so that MS-Hu6 in the formulation existed primarily as a monomer.
source: These data suggested that disodium-EDTA and L-methionine together improved colloidal stability, so that MS-Hu6 in the formulation existed primarily as a monomer.
evidence: The results section interprets the DLS data.

claim: Formulated MS-Hu6 showed a concentration–dependent linear increase in viscosity (11.3, 12, 15, 18.8 and 27.5 cP for 1, 10, 20, 50 and 100 mg/mL, respectively).
source: Compared with water (3 cP) and formulation buffer (5.4 cP), formulated MS-Hu6 showed a concentration–dependent linear increase in viscosity (11.3, 12, 15, 18.8 and 27.5 cP, respectively; Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section reports viscosity measurements from Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in viscosity likely resulted from the crowding of MS-Hu6 molecules that is expected at high antibody concentrations.
source: The increase in viscosity likely resulted from the crowding of MS-Hu6 molecules that is expected at high antibody concentrations (Raut and Kalonia, 2016).
evidence: The results section cites a reference for this interpretation.

claim: The viscosity of the formulation at all MS-Hu6 concentrations were within the acceptable industry standard (<50 cP).
source: However, importantly, the viscosity of the formulation at all MS-Hu6 concentrations were within the acceptable industry standard (<50 cP).
evidence: The results section compares viscosity values to industry standards.

claim: There was a concentration-dependent increase in turbidity absorbance, with a flattening at 100 mg/mL MS-Hu6 in formulation.
source: There was a concentration-dependent increase in absorbance, with a flattening at 100 mg/mL MS-Hu6 in formulation.
evidence: The results section reports turbidity data from Figure 3B.

claim: The increase in turbidity at 100 mg/mL is likely due to antibody crowding in solution and formation of reversible aggregates.
source: The increase at 100 mg/mL is likely due to antibody crowding in solution and formation of reversible aggregates; however, the latter phenomenon is not consequential in biopharmaceutical product development.
evidence: The results section interprets the turbidity increase.

claim: Reversible aggregates are not consequential in biopharmaceutical product development.
source: The increase at 100 mg/mL is likely due to antibody crowding in solution and formation of reversible aggregates; however, the latter phenomenon is not consequential in biopharmaceutical product development.
evidence: The results section states this industry perspective.

claim: The percent transmittance for each MS-Hu6 concentration was more than >99% at the three wavelengths (350, 540, and 595 nm).
source: In all, the percent transmittance for each concentration was more than >99% at the three wavelengths, suggesting that the formulations are clear between 0.2 and 50 mg/mL and slightly opalescent at 100 mg/mL.
evidence: The results section reports clarity data from Figure 3C.

claim: The formulations are clear between 0.2 and 50 mg/mL and slightly opalescent at 100 mg/mL.
source: In all, the percent transmittance for each concentration was more than >99% at the three wavelengths, suggesting that the formulations are clear between 0.2 and 50 mg/mL and slightly opalescent at 100 mg/mL.
evidence: The results section interprets the clarity data.

claim: All MS-Hu6 concentrations fall into the acceptable clarity categories of Ref I and II [3–6 Nephelometric Turbidity Units].
source: All concentrations fall into the acceptable clarity categories of Ref I and II [3–6 Nephelometric Turbidity Units] (European Pharmacopoeia, 2017).
evidence: The results section cites the European Pharmacopoeia for clarity standards.

claim: The predominant secondary structure in MS-Hu6 was regular β-sheets and unordered/random coils.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and through mathematical derivations of ellipticity (millidegrees) and mean residue ellipticity, analysis in the far UV region (190–240 nm), revealed that, as with other IgG molecules, the predominant secondary structure in MS-Hu6 was regular β-sheets and unordered/random coils (Kelly et al., 2005; Moreno et al., 2016; Vermeer et al., 1998).
evidence: The results section reports CD spectroscopy data from Figure 4A and cites references.

claim: There was no alteration in any secondary structure parameter in formulated MS-Hu6 versus MS-Hu6 in PBS (0.5 mg/mL).
source: Importantly, there was no alteration in any parameter in formulated MS-Hu6 versus MS-Hu6 in PBS (0.5 mg/mL).
evidence: The results section reports CD spectroscopy comparison from Figure 4A.

claim: The amide I band peak at 1637 cm–1 (intra–molecular β-sheets) and the random coil (1642–1657 cm–1) did not shift in FTIR, confirming maintenance of the native conformation in formulation.
source: The amide I band peak at 1637 cm–1, a surrogate for intra-molecular β-sheets, and the random coil structure peak at 1642–1657 cm–1 did not shift, confirming maintenance of the antibody's native conformation in formulation (Figure 4B).
evidence: The results section reports FTIR data from Figure 4B.

claim: MS-Hu6 displayed multi–domain transitions in Nano DSC, with the first transition representing unfolding of CH2 (Fc) domain (Tm >71 °C), the second representing Fab unfolding (Tm >80.30 °C), and a third CH3 (Fc) domain unfolding (Tm >85 °C).
source: MS-Hu6 displayed multi–domain transitions, with the first transition representing unfolding of CH2 (Fc) domain (Tm >71 °C), the second representing Fab unfolding (Tm >80.30 °C), and a third CH3 (Fc) domain unfolding (Tm >85 °C) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section reports Nano DSC data from Figure 4C.

claim: MS-Hu6 at 50 and 100 mg/ml had comparable Tms in Nano DSC, indicating that the overall structure is conformationally and thermally stable at high concentrations.
source: Both samples had comparable Tms, indicating that the overall structure is conformationally and thermally stable at high concentrations.
evidence: The results section interprets Nano DSC data from Figure 4C.

claim: The heat capacity required for the CH3 unfolding was ~two fold greater than Fab unfolding, and 7.73–8.52-fold greater than the CH2 transition.
source: Furthermore, the heat capacity required for the CH3 unfolding was ~two fold greater than Fab unfolding, and 7.73–8.52-fold greater than the CH2 transition.
evidence: The results section reports heat capacity data from Nano DSC.

claim: The heat capacity finding is consistent with what is observed for most IgG antibodies.
source: This latter finding is consistent with what is observed for most IgG antibodies (Ionescu et al., 2008; Ahrer et al., 2006; Garber and Demarest, 2007).
evidence: The results section cites references for this comparison.

claim: Baseline Tms for formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) without F/T were 69.55 ± 0.12°C and 79.35 ± 0.05°C for Fc and Fab, respectively.
source: Baseline Tms for formulated MS-Hu6 (100 mg/mL) without F/T were 69.55 ± 0.12°C and 79.35 ± 0.05°C for Fc and Fab, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports baseline Tm values from Figure 5A.

claim: After storage at –80 °C and thawing to 25 °C for three cycles, ΔTm values for both Fc and Fab domains revealed no significant difference between each cycle and baseline.
source: Calculations of ΔTm values for the both Fc and Fab domains, with each F/T cycle compared with baseline revealed no significant difference between each cycle and baseline.
evidence: The results section reports freeze-thaw data from Figure 5A.

claim: For samples stored at –80 °C and thawed to 37 °C over three cycles, while the Fc domain remained stable, there was a small, <1 °C, decrease in Fab Tm compared with samples without F/T.
source: In another experimental set, samples were stored at –80 °C and thawed to 37 °C, over three cycles. While the Fc domain remained stable, there was a small, <1 °C, decrease in Fab Tm compared with samples without F/T.
evidence: The results section reports freeze-thaw data from Figure 5A.

claim: The freeze-thaw results demonstrate that formulated MS-Hu6 is stable under extreme stress and that there is minimal or no aggregation or denaturation.
source: The results demonstrate that formulated MS-Hu6 is stable under extreme stress and that there is minimal or no aggregation or denaturation.
evidence: The results section interprets the freeze-thaw data.

claim: For three freeze-thaw cycles, the major volume peak (>99%) rh was found to be between 3–7 nm.
source: For three cycles, the major volume peak (>99%) rh was found to be between 3–7 nm (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section reports DLS data from Figure 5B.

claim: The Z–average rh for both freeze-thaw experimental sets for all cycles remained <10 nm (except cycle III of –80/25 °C), with PDIs being <1.
